  abstracts can qualify.

  systematic review, meeting report, editorial, commentary, perspective,
  correction, protocol, future-only proposal, method-only description, or
  atlas/database/cohort resource without a substantive current biological
  analysis and new results.
- `unclear`: the supplied text cannot distinguish these types.

types above. Do not infer `nonempirical` from missing sentences.

protocol, commentary, resource-only report, or completed original analysis.

substantive result clause; a clause cut off by an ellipsis does not qualify.

experiments, loci, proteins, molecular features, effects, or other substantive

mechanism, trajectory, mediator, marker, model, or intervention target.

background statements, a generic approach claim, or incomplete attribution,

In the current era of AD research, the gut-liver-brain BA axis emerges as a novel mechanistic framework linking systemic metabolic aging to neurodegeneration. This review examines the molecular pathways through which BA dysregulation influences aging and AD, emphasizing its therapeutic relevance and supporting the development of biomarker-based and precision medicine approaches for neurodegenerative disorders.</abstract>

<title>Mapping Genotype to Phenotype in Clonal Hematopoiesis Uncovers Downregulated MHC-II Molecules in DNMT3AR882 - Mutant Hematopoietic Stem Cells</title>
<abstract>Somatic mosaicism in blood cells, referred to as clonal hematopoiesis (CH), arises when hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) acquire somatic mutations that provide a substrate for clonal selection and subsequent clonal outgrowth over time. This condition becomes common with aging and is associated with adverse clinical outcomes related to mutated progenitor cells and increased inflammation. It has been shown that mutated clones have growth rates ranging from 5% to more than 50% per year and that they are acquired decades before they reach a substantial clone size. In CH, the most frequently mutated gene is DNMT3A encoding a de novo methyltransferase enzyme and the mutations are predominantly heterozygous, scattered throughout the three functional domains. In contrast, more than half of DNMT3A mutations in acute myeloid leukemia are missense alterations within the catalytic domain of the enzyme at residue R882. The high frequency of mutations at this specifc site suggests a gain-of-function activity. Beyond haploinsufficiency, the common heterozygous R882H allele creates an altered protein with dominant negative activity. Despite the increasing knowledge of how CH develops over time, the question regarding which mechanisms lead to clonal selection of mutant clones remains unresolved. Here, we performed single-cell multi-omics profiling of FACS-enriched CD34+ hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) and CD34- mature blood cells from n=9 DNMT3Amut peripheral blood samples with G-CSF mobilized HSPCs (autologous stem cell grafts) collected from multiple myeloma patients in remission. In total, 140,000 single cells were sequenced. Simultaneous mutation analysis enabled intra-sample comparison between DNMT3Amut and wild-type cells. Differential gene- and surface protein expression analysis (CITEseq) revealed downregulated MHC-II molecules in DNMT3AR882mut compared to wild-type HSCs. This observation was restricted to DNMT3AR882mut comparted to DNMT3ANon-R882mut samples. To validate this phenotype, we established a FACS-sorting strategy using HLA-DR, an MHC-II cell surface receptor involved in presenting peptides to CD4+ T cells, and compared mutant fractions (VAF) in HLA-DRlow vs. HLA-DRhigh FACS-sorted CD34+ HSPCs by digital-droplet PCR, thereby confirming an up to 2.5-fold higher DNMT3AR882mut fraction in HLA-DRlow sorted HSPCs. <title>Mapping Genotype to Phenotype in Clonal Hematopoiesis Uncovers Downregulated MHC-II Molecules in DNMT3AR882 - Mutant Hematopoietic Stem Cells</title>
<abstract>Somatic mosaicism in blood cells, referred to as clonal hematopoiesis (CH), arises when hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) acquire somatic mutations that provide a substrate for clonal selection and subsequent clonal outgrowth over time. This condition becomes common with aging and is associated with adverse clinical outcomes related to mutated progenitor cells and increased inflammation. In contrast, more than half of DNMT3A mutations in acute myeloid leukemia are missense alterations within the catalytic domain of the enzyme at residue R882. The high frequency of mutations at this specifc site suggests a gain-of-function activity. Beyond haploinsufficiency, the common heterozygous R882H allele creates an altered protein with dominant negative activity. Despite the increasing knowledge of how CH develops over time, the question regarding which mechanisms lead to clonal selection of mutant clones remains unresolved. Here, we performed single-cell multi-omics profiling of FACS-enriched CD34+ hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) and CD34- mature blood cells from n=9 DNMT3Amut peripheral blood samples with G-CSF mobilized HSPCs (autologous stem cell grafts) collected from multiple myeloma patients in remission. In total, 140,000 single cells were sequenced. Simultaneous mutation analysis enabled intra-sample comparison between DNMT3Amut and wild-type cells. Differential gene- and surface protein expression analysis (CITEseq) revealed downregulated MHC-II molecules in DNMT3AR882mut compared to wild-type HSCs. This observation was restricted to DNMT3AR882mut comparted to DNMT3ANon-R882mut samples. To validate this phenotype, we established a FACS-sorting strategy using HLA-DR, an MHC-II cell surface receptor involved in presenting peptides to CD4+ T cells, and compared mutant fractions (VAF) in HLA-DRlow vs. HLA-DRhigh FACS-sorted CD34+ HSPCs by digital-droplet PCR, thereby confirming an up to 2.5-fold higher DNMT3AR882mut fraction in HLA-DRlow sorted HSPCs. We have previously shown that HSPCs are capable of activating CD4+ T cells upon presentation of both, endogenous and exogenous antigens via MHC-II and that the presentation of immunogenic antigens via MHC-II by HSPCs mediates bidirectional interactions with antigen-specific CD4+ T cells. Therefore, we hypothesize that the observed downregulation of MHC-II expression in DNMT3AR882mut HSCs can alter the activation of CD4+ T cells, which can functionally impact the development of CH over time. We performed multi-parameter flow cytometry to characterize MHC-II expression on HSPCs and progenitor cell populations. Consistent with our human single-cell data, we observed that MHC-II (I-A/I-E) expression on HSPC subpopulations collected from mice with monoallelic DNMT3AR882H expression was downregulated compared to wild-type mice. In contrast, there was no difference at the progenitor cell level. To understand whether the observed downregulation of MHC-II molecules impacts the antigen-specific activation of CD4+ T cells, we co-cultured FACS-sorted HSPCs with CD4+ T cells from OT-II mice that express transgenic T cell receptors specifically recognizing the chicken ovalbumin (OVA329-339 peptide), when presented via MHC-II. Our preliminary analysis revealed that despite lower MHC-II expression, DNMT3AR882H HSPCs are still capable of activating CD4+ T cells in vitro. <abstract>Background Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) is the most common histological subtype of lung cancer and remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. <abstract>Objectives Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have pinpointed several risk loci linked to thyroid cancer; however, the discovery of new plasma proteins implicated in immunosenescence continues to pose significant challenges. This study aims to uncover novel plasma proteins tied to aging, potentially contributing to thyroid cancer, utilizing diverse investigative methodologies. Subsequently, we conducted a meta-analysis on the relationship between Hannum DNA methylation age and thyroid cancer risk, which identified 138 potential risk loci through FUMA. Additionally, proteomics and transcriptomics collectively identified 6 potential targets related to immunosenescence and thyroid cancer. Subsequently, Bulk-seq results indicated differential expression of GFRA2 and LILRA2 genes in thyroid cancer. Finally, analyses from an independent cohort at the Second Affiliated Hospital of Chongqing Medical University also demonstrated high expression of LILRA2 in thyroid cancer patients. Conclusions This study identified novel plasma proteins associated with immunosenescence that may be linked to thyroid cancer development. STABILITY CONTRACT

ORDERED SCOPE TABLE

1. `report_type`

- `empirical_primary`: substantive current biological/health analysis and new
  results, including public-data analysis, secondary analysis of completed
  experiments, model development on real biological data, or an original
  conference abstract.
- `nonempirical`: review, meeting report, editorial, commentary, perspective,
  protocol, future proposal, method-only description, resource, or no
  substantive current biological analysis and results.
- `unclear`: supplied text cannot resolve type.

A visible ellipsis or search-result truncation makes report type `unclear`
unless the visible text itself explicitly identifies a review, protocol,
commentary, resource-only report, or completed original analysis. Title words
such as `exploring`, `insights`, `toward`, `mechanism`, or `identifying` do
not establish completion. An empirical override requires a complete visible
current-author analysis predicate or a complete visible substantive result
clause; a clause cut off by an ellipsis does not qualify.

A truncated record is `empirical_primary` when its current-report title states
that an analysis `reveals/identifies/finds` a result, or its fragment says `we
performed/analyzed/analysed/profiled` and names an analysis or result. This
does not override an explicit review, protocol, commentary, or resource-only
description.

New substantive numerical findings attributed to the current report or its
named current consortium/project establish `empirical_primary`, even when
goals or resource access are also described.

A title containing `review`, `systematic review`, or a misspelled variant is
still `empirical_primary` when the abstract says the current authors performed
a new public-data/bioinformatics analysis and reports its own substantive or
numerical Results. Literature searching, study selection, evidence synthesis,
and summaries of included studies remain `nonempirical`.

If report type is not empirical primary, set biological scope, aging
relevance, and multi-omics to `not_assessed`.

2. `bio_health_scope`

Use `yes` for humans, animals, cells, tissues, microorganisms, molecular
biology, disease, health, lifespan, or another biological system; `no` for
purely non-biological work; `unclear` when unstated. If this value is not
`yes`, set aging and multi-omics to `not_assessed`.

3. `aging_process_relevance`

This is candidate retention. Use `yes` when the current report analyzes a
construct that the authors explicitly frame as aging, ageing, biological age,
or an aging-related biological process. The construct may be an exposure,
outcome, phenotype, group contrast, mechanism, trajectory, marker, model, or
intervention target.

Positive `yes` patterns:

- biological/epigenetic age, age acceleration, aging clock or trajectory,
  longevity, lifespan, healthspan, rejuvenation, geroprotection, senolysis;
- chronological-age or young/adult/aged comparisons only when the current
  report explicitly interprets a result as an effect, mechanism, trajectory,
  or process of aging, such as `aging exacerbates Y`, `effect of aging on Y`,
  or `age-associated molecular mechanisms`;
- a current-result contrast explicitly comparing a disease, intervention,
  exposure, or molecular phenotype with `healthy aging` or `normal aging`,
  including an analyzed healthy-aging cohort;
- frailty, telomere length, thymic atrophy, or another measured phenotype
  explicitly called a marker, indicator, onset, manifestation, model, or
  component of biological aging;
- cellular senescence measured, compared, induced, reversed, or targeted,
  including measured senescence-associated markers plus a reported senescent
  or senescent-like phenotype;
- an intervention tested against a phenotype explicitly framed as aging.

A positive pattern overrides proxy ambiguity, including for an induced model
or a study that also analyzes disease.

Chronological-age sampling alone is not an aging-process analysis. `At
different ages`, `with age`, `as animals aged`, `age-dependent`, or
`progressive` remains `no` when it only stages development, disease
progression, treatment response, or model characterization and the report does
not interpret the result as aging biology. An age-related disease alone does
not supply that interpretation. An explicit current-result comparison with
`healthy aging` or `normal aging` is the positive pattern above; a background
mention without such a comparison is not.

Use `no` only when a complete record has no positive pattern and age is only a
covariate, demographic/recruitment label, older cohort, developmental time,
age-related disease context, disease-model progression, or background; when it
concerns persistence or durability rather than aging; or when it only predicts
chronological age.

Disease survival or time-to-event is not longevity/aging unless the authors
frame it that way. An incidental named age-related disease/tumor feature, such
as an age-related mutational signature in an analysis where age is merely
adjusted for, does not make aging a study construct.

Use `unclear` only when an aging-linked proxy is named but its current analysis
is unresolved. Senescence-related gene labels without a measured senescent
state are `unclear`. A target described only as senescence-inducing,
senescence-associated, or senescence-related without a measured, compared,
induced, reversed, or targeted senescent state is also `unclear`. If aging is
not `yes`, set multi-omics to `not_assessed`.

A database-curated aging-gene list or pathway/enrichment annotation returning
aging, longevity, or cellular-senescence terms is also `unclear` when the
current report does not measure an aging phenotype, trajectory, state,
intervention target, or process.

- `no`: complete record clearly uses zero or one modality and makes no

- `unclear`: attribution to the current report is unresolved.

Future or ongoing multi-omics does not count. Two GWAS traits or multiple
assays of one modality remain one. Clinical variables, imaging, flow
cytometry, and routine biomarkers are not separate molecular modalities.
Always return `omics_layers=[]`.
An empirical title where `multiomics`, `multi-omics`, or `multi-omic`
directly modifies the analyzed phenotype, exposure, signature, age, or
analysis is a current-report multi-omics claim and is `yes`, including

modality unless its underlying molecular data are analyzed. Comparing a
clinical/LLM prediction with epigenetic-age values and separately identifying
proteomic biomarkers is not multi-omics unless those molecular layers are
analytically connected in the current report.

Apply this lexically. Do not downgrade a match because the study is profiling
